extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in linguistics, comedy studies, and discourse/semantic analysis (e.g., thesis authors applying formal semantics to humour)
extracted.subtask_description: A formal, theory-driven method for analysing jokes using model theory/formal semantics, Gricean pragmatics, and Austinian performatives; applied to short selections of Bo Burnham's comedy. The output is an ontology-driven description of who/what is in a joke and an account of speaker intention and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign comedic categories to a given joke
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign one or more comedic categories to a given joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step 1 of the proposed approach: label the joke's comedic type (what type of jokes are made) as a starting point for analysis. This helps frame subsequent ontology and pragmatic analysis of the joke's 'comedic force' (the substance of the joke).

rubrics_metrics.name: Create ontology for the state-of-affairs (OS = ES + IS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct an ontology for the state-of-affairs by summing the extension (E) and intension (I): OS = ES + IS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ontology represents 'what is in the joke' (entities, participants) and 'what is happening' (actions, properties). Be explicit about what is included; the thesis warns that different interpreters may produce different ontologies and that including everything leads to arbitrarily large ontologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit ontology to relevant entities and actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Include only relevant elements in the extension and intension when building an ontology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid arbitrarily large or infinite ontologies, the paper prescribes including only entities and actions relevant to the analysis of the joke (examples contrast minimal E/I vs exhaustive lists like arms, fingers, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use denotation assignment function (Fda) to map ontology to meta-language
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply a denotation assignment function Fda: O → OM to transform ontology elements into meta-language entities and predicates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fda(E) = N (entities) and Fda(I) = P (predicates). Entities and predicates are given meta-language representations (entities lower-case, predicates denoted and potentially primed). Example: Fda(WOMAN1) = alice, Fda(APPLE) = apple, Fda(EAT) = eat; then eat = {(alice, apple)} as an ordered tuple.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use translation-language mapping between object-language and meta-language (TLang)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a translation-language function TLang : OLang → MLang (and inverse TLang^{-1}) to convert object-language sentences into meta-language representations and back.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat translation as a function: TLang(sentence) = x (a meta-language representation), assign truth value to x, and use TLang^{-1} to present the interpreted (sentence, truth-value) pair. This formalises truth-conditional interpretation of jokes/utterances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent participants and relations using sets and ordered n-tuples
rubrics_metrics.description: Model entities and relations with set-theoretic objects and ordered n-tuples to capture argument structure and role order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predicates are n-place relations whose truth depends on whether the ordered n-tuple of entities is a member of the predicate set. Order matters (e.g., (alice, apple) ≠ (apple, alice)). Use ordered tuples to represent who does what to whom in the joke's state-of-affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate extension vs intension
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat extension (E) as the set of objects/entities and intension (I) as the set of properties/actions in a state-of-affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the distinction when constructing ontologies: extension gives the physical participants, intension gives actions/properties. Use numbered subscripts for identical lexemes that refer to distinct entities (e.g., FISH1, FISH2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Number homonyms/identical lexemes to disambiguate meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Handle homonyms and repeated lexemes by numbering alternative meanings or repeated occurrences in the translation (wi^n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the same lexeme appears with different senses or multiple referents, use numbered subscripts in the meta-language/Fda output to avoid conflation (shown in examples with fish/fish and die=laugh/die).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply truth-conditional semantics to predicates
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge predicate truth by membership: an n-place predicate Pn is true iff the ordered n-tuple (e1, e2, ..., en) is in the set denoted by Pn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ties the meta-language representation to truth-values: e.g., (Alice eats an apple, true) because (alice, apple) ∈ eat. Use this to state whether the described state-of-affairs obtains for the joke utterance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and categorize performatives (Austinian analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify performative utterances and classify locutionary/illocutionary/perlocutionary acts to analyse what the speaker is doing by saying something.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Austin's framework to capture the action-performing aspect of utterances (e.g., 'Watch out!' as a warning). The thesis applies performative analysis in conjunction with Gricean analysis to capture intended effects and actions on stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define felicity/success conditions for performatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide explicit criteria for when a performative is successfully performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The thesis notes a shortcoming: the need for a precise and rigorous outline of what must be true for a performative to count as 'successfully done'. Analysts should state these felicity conditions when claiming a performative has occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Grice's Cooperative Principle to infer intention and meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Grice's Cooperative Principle ('Make your conversational contribution such as is required...') to analyse the utterer's intentions and conversational implicatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine the model-theoretic description of 'what is said' with Gricean reasoning to determine 'what is meant'. This is step 4 of the formal approach and is essential for decoding implied comedic meaning and speaker intention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxim — Quantity (informativeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make your contribution as informative as required for the exchange; do not be more informative than required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the two submaxims to evaluate whether extra information in a joke or delivery is appropriate, excessive, or intentionally over/under-informative (example: adding 'has not been to prison yet' may flout or violate Quantity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxim — Quality (truth/evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not say what you believe to be false; do not say that for which you lack adequate evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether statements within the joke are being presented as true or are knowingly false/unsupported—useful to identify irony, sarcasm, or deliberate untruth for comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxim — Relation (relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether utterances and stage actions are relevant to the conversational/topic trajectory; deliberate irrelevance or apparent non sequiturs can generate conversational implicatures exploited for humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxim — Manner (clarity and presentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid obscurity and ambiguity, be brief (avoid unnecessary prolixity), and be orderly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how something is said (tone, timing, brevity, order). Delivery features—ambiguity, obscurity, or deliberate prolixity—are part of comedic technique and should be coded under Manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish conventional vs nonconventional implications (and conversational implicatures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate literal/conventional meaning from nonconventional readings and conversational implicatures arising from the Cooperative Principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use context and ontology-transformation to decide whether a statement's meaning is conventional (literal) or a conversational implication (e.g., 'Albert is dying' interpreted as laughing in context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for cultural/contextual variability and vagueness in Gricean maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise that maxims are vague and culturally variable; their application must be context-sensitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The thesis flags critiques: maxims can be underspecified, and cultural norms affect cooperative expectations. Analysts should justify Gricean inferences and be cautious about over-generalising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make interpreter assumptions explicit (interpreter variability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly state interpreter-specific choices because different interpreters of the same state-of-affairs can yield different ontologies and analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The thesis formalises this: for distinct interpreters In(OSk) ≠ Im(OSk). Document assumptions about what is included in E and I, how Fda is constructed, and contextual cues relied upon for pragmatic inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological scope: qualitative sampling limits generalisability; prefer quantitative for corpus claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit about methodological scope: qualitative analysis on a small sample cannot definitively establish an artist's full 'comedic type' or 'comedic force'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The thesis concludes the formal qualitative approach is useful for illustrating elements of joke construction but recommends a quantitative approach (analyzing the artist's full corpus) for stronger generalisations about overall comedic type/force.
